results.title: Introduction to Part 1 of the Themed Issue, ‘Racism and Colonialism in Hegel's Philosophy’: Rationale and Topics
results.abstract: It is increasingly realized today that Western modernity has not only promoted progressive ideals such as scientific thought, human rights and democratic political systems. Its history is also marked by a much darker side, one of brutal conquest, biological and cultural destruction, enslavement and exploitation of non-European peoples in the context of European colonialism. This dark side of Western modernity was legitimized by pro-colonial ideologies of property, war, civilization, progress and race. Such ideologies emerged in areas like jurisprudence and philosophy since the 16th century, often building on views from classical antiquity (Pagden 1995). They shaped academic paradigms such as ‘scientific racism’, colonial anthropology and Orientalism in the 19th and early 20th centuries, and in many ways continue to influence contemporary societies and their academic practices.

Colonial Slavery, the Lord-Bondsman Dialectic, and the St Louis Hegelians
results.abstract: Abstract Hegel's lord-bondsman dialectic has been of especially great interest to progressive and radical Hegelians—broadly speaking, politically left-leaning interpreters of Hegel who object to certain social hierarchies and demand their abolition. They read Hegel as giving an account of how ‘lordship’ over others is an inherently unstable and unsatisfying social formation, even for its supposed beneficiaries. Marxists, feminists and post-colonial theorists have all found inspiration in Hegel's analysis of the lord and bondsman by applying it to concrete relations of oppression, such as capitalism, patriarchy, or racism. In contrast, recent scholarship on Hegel's views on race and colonialism has cast doubt on whether his systematic political philosophy and philosophy of history can be of similar use to progressives. Hegel was undeniably a Eurocentric thinker, but philosophers like Robert Bernasconi and Alison Stone have convincingly shown that he was also a racist and a defender of colonialism. Crucially, however, few of the scholars who write on Hegel's pro-colonialism have analysed this feature of Hegel's thought in connection with the lord-bondsman dialectic. In this article, I argue for two connected theses. First, I argue that contrary to the hopes of some progressive defenders of Hegel, we cannot easily separate the lord-bondsman dialectic from Hegel's pro-colonialism. This is because Hegel himself appealed to the lord-bondsman dialectic to argue that colonial slavery educated its victims, and could therefore be temporarily justified. Second, I argue that this pro-colonial reading of the dialectic, though largely ignored by contemporary interpreters, was in fact recognized and embraced by a group of Hegelians in North America known as the St Louis Hegelians. They used the lord-bondsman dialectic as a basis for a qualified defence of pre-Civil War American slavery.

results.title: Rebecca Comay and Bart Zantvoort (eds.). Hegel and Resistance: History, Politics and Dialectics. London: Bloomsbury, 2018. ISBN-10: 1350003646. Pp. 205. £85.00 (hbk).
results.abstract: In a world where capitalism and the liberal state are (i) increasingly failing to provide decent living conditions for the working classes, (ii) continuing to reinforce different forms of racism, sexism and neo-colonialism, and (iii) carrying out an unparalleled destruction of the environment threatening all human life on this planet, what does Hegel have to offer us? If one starts from the premise that our current forms of social life need to be fundamentally reorganized to secure anything like a decent life for our species, it might be natural to suspect that Hegel—the quintessential philosopher of synthesis and reconciliation—would not be especially helpful in such a critical endeavour. Perhaps this is why, as Bart Zantvoort’s introduction rightly points out, from the early analytical philosophy of Moore and Russell to the post-structuralism of Foucault and Deleuze, ‘the history of modern philosophy can be read as a history of resistance to Hegel’ (1). One of the goals of Rebecca Comay and Bart Zantvoort’s edited collection seems to be a productive response to this challenge, aiming to show that Hegel’s thought on resistance does indeed offer something valuable for contemporary philosophy. It does this by collecting a series of essays exploring the theme of resistance in various aspects of Hegel’s philosophy, from his method to the role he sees for resistance in politics. After Zantvoort’s scene-setting introduction, the chapters in Part 1 discuss Hegel’s method. Frank Ruda’s ‘Hegel, Resistance and Method’ argues that resistance is inherent to Hegel’s method itself, with a particular focus on Hegel’s discussion of the speculative sentence. Thereafter, Rebecca Comay’s ‘Resistance and Repetition: Hegel and Freud’ compares the role of resistance in the development of consciousness in the Phenomenology to its role in Freudian psychoanalysis. Rocío Zambrana’s ‘Dialectics as Resistance: Hegel, Benjamin, Adorno’ compares and contrasts the dialectics in the work of Hegel, Walter Benjamin and Theodor Adorno. The chapters in Part 2 examine different kinds of resistance in Hegel’s philosophy, with Howard Caygill’s ‘The Spirit of Resistance and its Fate’ exploring the role of resistance in Hegel’s thought from the early theological writings to the Science of Logic. results.title: Hegel, Haiti and revolution: the post-colonial moment
results.abstract: Abstract Susan Buck-Morss’s argument that the Haitian Revolution embodied the most universal aspect of the French Revolution, namely the quest for universal freedom, relies on the supposed references to Haiti in the master–slave dialogue in Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit. The revolution’s lodgement at the core of this foundational text of Enlightenment universalism is, for her, about as convincing a demonstration as one can have of the universal significance of the Haitian Revolution. Marxists have opposed her venture, and demonstrated their hostility to post-colonial thinking, principally by claiming that the master–slave is an expression of European class conflict. This paper agrees with Buck-Morss that the Haitian Revolution critically affirmed the principle of universal freedom and, indeed, pushed the revolution in France and Europe in a radical direction. A better affirmation of the universal significance of the Haitian Revolution than the thoughts of Hegel is possible. The latter do not actually provide such affirmation, because racism, Eurocentrism and a hostility to political radicalism are fundamental aspects of Hegel’s thought. The alternative affirmation can be found in Marxist analysis. This paper outlines such an analysis, and concludes that post-colonialism of Buck-Morss’s sort is no substitute for the perspective provided by historical materialism.

results.abstract: it is a call for self-determination, Du Bois’s consistent championing of which is shown to be not just a vehicle of reform, but also a crucial corrective to the idea that Black people have been passive observers of history, deprived of agency, rather than active participants and engines of progress. Throughout the book, Basevich successfully establishes Du Bois’s place among the great philosophers and political thinkers of history, building bridges, as she puts it, between Du Bois and earlier thinkers such as Kant and Hegel. As Errol Henderson writes in The Revolution Will Not Be Theorized: Cultural Revolution in the Black Power Era (State University of New York Press 2019), although there has been a marked increase in research and writing about Black activists, these figures “are typically acknowledged for their activism, but rarely for their acumen as revolutionary theorists” (ix). This book does not fall into the same trap, as it consecrates Du Bois’s thoughts, philosophies, and theories in the global history of ideas. The author also describes some of the contemporary opposition to these ideas, and she unpicks the debates in which Du Bois himself engaged— most notably, with Booker T. Washington. She uses these debates as a springboard to argue for a contemporary model of activism that both learns from the past and empowers a new generation of organizers and leaders. One thing that is perhaps missing, especially from the earlier chapters, is an examination of how Du Bois’s philosophies and praxis were formed by his years as a student, particularly by his time in Germany. Given the importance placed on sociology, it might have been useful to see how spending time in Europe set him apart from other US scholars. Later in the book, a reader familiar with recent work on Du Bois might lament the absence of a fuller exploration of his embrace of Marxism and ideological shift to the left in the latter half of his life. From his first visit to the Soviet Union in 1926 and throughout the subsequent decades, this move leftward is a palpable and important feature of Du Bois’s work and thought. This shift culminated, in many ways, in Black Reconstruction in America (1935), a masterpiece and turning point in the history of scholarship surrounding slavery, the Civil War, emancipation, and Reconstruction. It is, as BurdenStelly has argued, representative both of his embrace of left-wing ideology and Marxist thought and of the departure from his earlier liberal positions (“W. E. B. Du Bois in the Tradition of Radical Blackness: Radicalism, Repression, and Mutual Comradeship, 1930–1960,” in Carson, Horne, & Sinitiere, ed., Socialism and Democracy in W. E. B. Du Bois’s Life, Thought, and Legacy [The Research Group on Socialism and Democracy 2019], 183). To understand Du Bois’s significance as a historian requires engagement with this seminal—but much maligned—work, and it must be said that Basevich does so admirably in the fifth chapter. She aptly sums up the key idea of this epic tome, stating, “the principle of universal democratic self-determination remained an ‘abstract’ republican ideal until black historical agents disrupted the prevailing institutional order in the Americas and rooted out the central contradiction between republics’ racial realities and its republican self-definition” (133). This argument was vociferously disputed at the time by historians who still clung to the Lost Cause myth and other white-supremacist interpretations of American history, and it is resisted now, most obviously through the manufactured controversy over Critical Race Theory. Basevich ably demonstrates the centrality of Black Reconstruction to Du Bois’s importance today, as she does with the wide range of Du Bois’s writings on which she draws. She deploys his words from books, poems, essays, articles, editorials, and correspondence, alongside her own, to help bolster the arguments of each chapter and to provide a rhetorical flourish to what is already a fluent and eloquent text. Basevich is herself a poet, and this comes across in her elegantly and often stirringly written book, which is both a work of well-reasoned scholarship and a call to action. I believe that this book adds greatly to the already vast body of scholarship on W. E. B. Du Bois and demonstrates that there are always new areas of his life and legacy to explore. A reader already familiar with the story of Du Bois’s life will learn a great deal, as would anyone with an interest in Black history and the contemporary struggle over racism and inequality in America. One feels a sense of despair and outrage as Basevich recounts the many egregious acts of violence and oppression that haunt America’s past and present, but she leaves room for hope that things can improve, provided that the activism and leadership embodied by Du Bois continue, and that the country as a whole faces the truth described in his work and follows his guiding star along the path to reform.

But while recognizing the weaknesses in Goldberg’s arcane philosophy, he deems it to have been ‘a powerful and imaginative response to the emerging ideology of state-based racism in Weimar Germany’ (p. 119) and the means whereby Israel might have been able to transform itself into ‘the metaphysical folk group’, i.e. ‘the vehicle for the final goal of history – when the totality of humanity will embody the image of God’. In Chapter 4 (pp. 118–61), Professor Rosenstock elaborates Goldberg’s ideas via a detailed discussion of Die Wirklichkeit der Hebräer that the average gentile reader will find hard to understand. In doing so, he stresses, however, that ‘Goldberg [was] not claiming Jewish racial superiority’ but arguing that the Jews had ‘rejected racial gods for the one universal God’ in order to preserve their cultural identity and sense of mission down the ages (p. 155). Chapter 5 (pp. 162–203) begins with an explanation of the differences between Goldberg’s and Scholem’s understanding of Jewish history that caused such hostility between them (pp. 163–73) and the relationship between Walter Benjamin and the Goldberg circle (pp. 178–81). The rest of the chapter is taken up by a disquisition on Goldberg’s book (1935) on the Sephardic Torah scholar Moses Maimonides (1135– 1204). It begins with ‘a broad overview of the history of Judaism’ (p. 181) before focusing more sharply on Maimonides’ philosophy and substituting 14 propositions of Goldberg’s own devising (pp. 184–92) – which culminate in the assertion that God ‘wants humanity to work together with him to build a new tabernacle where his glory can dwell in the midst of the world’ (p. 189) – for Maimonides’ ‘thirteen articles of faith’. The modern secular reader may find Goldberg the esoteric mystagogue at best hard to follow and at worst not worth following because of his obscurity. So it is worth emphasizing that Chapter 5 is comparatively accessible for gentiles and non-specialists and administers the coup de grâce to the idea that Goldberg can be ‘aligned with the reactionary political philosophies of [Carl] Schmitt and [Martin] Heidegger’ (p. 197). Conversely, Goldberg’s historical optimism may be obscure, but it permits Professor Rosenstock to liken him to a ‘Jewish Hegel breaking into the static nature of Kant’s conditions’ for whom ‘the goal of creation is to allow God’s infinite power to find expression within the finite realm so that his justice can be reconciled with his omnipotence’ (p. 192). Or, in other words, Professor Rosenstock has assured Goldberg of a well-defined place in modern German-Jewish cultural history, and it will be a long time before another scholar has the patience and specialist knowledge to better his magisterial work.
